courseTitle: How IT Teams Work: Agile, Waterfall, Scrum, Kanban & Software Releases

slots.practicalActivity: Picture a small internal request: 'Sales wants a dashboard showing revenue by region, updated daily.' Write out how that request would move through a Waterfall process (one long requirements → design → build → test → release chain) versus a Scrum process (broken into 1-2 week sprints). Then write 3 user stories for the dashboard in the 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]' shape, each with at least one concrete acceptance criterion.
slots.deliverable: A short written comparison of how the same request would play out under Waterfall vs. Scrum, plus 3 properly-formatted user stories with acceptance criteria.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a Kanban board (on paper or in a spreadsheet) with Backlog, To Do, In Progress, Review, and Done columns, and place the 3 user stories from the previous hour into Backlog. Set a WIP limit of 2 for In Progress and explain in writing why that limit helps rather than slows the team down. Then diagram the Dev → QA → UAT → Production path one of those stories would travel, noting who signs off at each handoff.
slots.deliverable: A populated Kanban board with a stated WIP limit and justification, plus a labeled Dev → QA → UAT → Production diagram for one user story.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a free GitHub account and a new repository (or use one you already have). Run the real clone → branch → edit → add → commit → push workflow from the lesson on a small test file: git clone, git checkout -b fix-report-filter, edit the file, git add ., git commit -m with a specific message (not 'fixed stuff'), git push, then open a pull request against main. Write a one-paragraph explanation of where a CI/CD pipeline would automatically test and deploy that change after the PR merges.
slots.deliverable: A real GitHub pull request (screenshot or link) showing a branch, a specific commit message, and an open PR, plus a written paragraph placing CI/CD in that workflow.

slots.practicalActivity: Start the Castlebridge Retail capstone from the lesson: the sales director's request is 'Our regional managers keep asking me for last month's numbers by email. I need a dashboard that shows revenue by region and by product category, updated automatically, so they can check it themselves.' Write the full set of user stories (revenue-by-region, revenue-by-category, automatic refresh), each with acceptance criteria, and place them on your Kanban board from hour 2.
slots.deliverable: A complete, acceptance-criteria-backed backlog of user stories for the Castlebridge Retail dashboard request, placed on your Kanban board.

slots.practicalActivity: Finish the Castlebridge Retail capstone end to end: write a short QA test plan for each story including at least one edge case (what happens when a region has zero sales?), write a one-paragraph UAT sign-off in the sales director's voice, write a short, specific release note (not 'various improvements'), and finally write up how you'd investigate and communicate about a simulated production incident where last month's numbers show as zero for one region.
slots.deliverable: A finished capstone packet: QA test plan with an edge case, a UAT sign-off paragraph, specific release notes, and a written production-incident response plan.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can read and work inside a real IT team's workflow — writing acceptance-criteria-backed user stories, tracking work on a Kanban board, using Git/GitHub's clone-branch-commit-push-PR cycle, and explaining how a change moves from Dev through QA, UAT, and a monitored production release.
